title: Jerusalem Stands Against Assyria
overview: King Hezekiah defends Jerusalem against the mighty Assyrian empire, survives a deadly illness, and is then tested by his own success.

parts.label: Hezekiah prepares the city (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: Assyria, the superpower of the day, invaded Judah around 701 BC, so Hezekiah blocked the springs outside Jerusalem to leave the attackers thirsty while he rebuilt the walls and made weapons. He told his people the enemy had only human strength, while they had God on their side.

parts.label: Assyria's war of words (vv. 9-19)
parts.note: While besieging Lachish, a major town southwest of Jerusalem, Sennacherib sent officials to shout in Hebrew so the ordinary people on the wall would understand and lose heart. They even twisted Hezekiah's religious reform, his closing of local shrines so worship centered on the one altar in Jerusalem, into proof that Judah's God was offended and would not help.

parts.label: Prayer and rescue (vv. 20-23)
parts.note: After Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah prayed, the text says an angel struck down the Assyrian army and Sennacherib went home humiliated; what physically happened is unknown, and some suggest a sudden plague. His murder by his own sons actually came about twenty years later, but the writer tells it here to round off the story.

parts.label: Illness, pride and humility (vv. 24-26)
parts.note: Hezekiah nearly died and was healed with a sign, which the fuller account in 2 Kings describes as a shadow moving backward. The writer says he then grew proud without saying exactly how, but he humbled himself, so the judgment was held back during his lifetime.

parts.label: Wealth, water and a test (vv. 27-31)
parts.note: His riches and building works are presented as signs of God's favor, and his tunnel bringing Gihon spring water inside the city still exists, with an ancient Hebrew inscription found carved in it. When envoys from Babylon came asking about his healing, God left him on his own to reveal what was truly in his heart.

parts.label: Hezekiah's death (vv. 32-33)
parts.note: The writer points readers to other records, including Isaiah's, for the rest of his story. He was buried with honor among David's royal descendants, and his son Manasseh became king.

think: When you face a threat far bigger than yourself, how do you balance doing everything practical you can with whatever else you lean on for hope?
